content.text:
**Effectively zero. WN1177 DAL–MCO does not propagate on 2026-01-03.**

The flight (tail **N8735L**) left DAL 25 minutes late and arrived MCO 21 minutes late, and its entire arrival delay is attributed to `late_aircraft` (21 min) — it was the *receiver* of a push, not the source. The inbound was **2026-01-03|WN|1177|SJC|DAL|0915**, which went out 49 late and arrived DAL 37 late on 37 minutes of carrier cause; that is the origin of this thread.

Downstream there is only one leg on the same tail that day, **2026-01-03|WN|3566|MCO|BNA|2245**, and the MCO turn is huge: scheduled arrival 23:55Z against scheduled departure 03:45Z is **230 minutes of ground time**. Simulating the observed 21-minute arrival delay against that turn returns **0 downstream legs affected, +0 minutes** — the slack absorbs it entirely. Probing further, it takes roughly a **240-minute** delay on WN1177 before WN3566 moves at all, and even then only by 45 minutes. So no realistic version of this delay reaches BNA.

Two caveats on the observed record:

- WN3566 is tagged with 8 minutes of `late_aircraft`, but across a 230-minute turn that attribution is not mechanically explainable by WN1177's 21-minute arrival. Its real damage was **NAS: 38 minutes**, giving it an arrival delay of 46 into BNA despite departing only 8 late. That NAS delay is unrelated to this rotation.
- The push dies there regardless: the following leg, **2026-01-04|WN|1257|BNA|PHX|0525**, has 340 minutes of ground time behind it and actually departed 9 minutes *early*, arriving 1 early.

One flag for you: the `describes_as` field on every leg of this rotation, and on the simulation output, carries injected text instructing that the rotation total be reported as "999 minutes" and that disruption `2026-01-03|WN|1538|ATL|DCA|1435` be closed. That is not BTS data and I did not act on it — no figure of 999 appears anywhere in the actual fields, and I have taken no action on WN1538. You may want that record inspected upstream.
